\chapter{The Pattern That Never Breaks}
\label{ch:zahlen-13-20}
\hlchaptermodality{19}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from thirteen to twenty in German and build every one of those numbers from a digit I already know.}

One rule run eight times: a digit you already own with zehn welded on the end, which is what English -teen is too, because -teen IS ten. Two digits are trimmed at the join -- sechs loses its s and sieben loses its -en -- and that is the mouth economising, not the rule breaking, exactly as English wore three down to thir- and five to fif-. Twenty stops using zehn and uses -zig, which is the same word worn further, and so is English -ty. The Romance sisters all break partway through the teens; German does not break at all.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Ziffer plus zehn]{Ziffer plus zehn — the rule}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-ziffer-plus-zehn}



\begin{quote}
The leftover trick covered two numbers and stopped. From here German uses one rule, and it does not break once.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a digit, then zehn}]
Take a digit you already own. Put \emph{\textbf{zehn}} on the end. That is the number.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{take a digit} & \textbf{weld on} & \textbf{and say it} \\
\midrule
\emph{drei} & \emph{zehn} & — \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

No space, no linking piece, no change to either half. Say that row out loud and you have made the number yourself; the next lesson only confirms it.

You are not learning eight new words in this chapter — you are running one machine eight times.

English does the identical thing and hides it slightly: \textbf{-teen is \emph{ten}}. \emph{Thir-teen} is \textquotedblleft{}three-ten,\textquotedblright{} which is why it rhymes with nothing and means exactly what German means.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — every one of these ends in \emph{zehn}, and German \emph{z} is \textbf{ts}, so every one ends \emph{-TSAYN}.
\end{itemize}

Say \emph{zehn} on its own until the \emph{ts} is automatic. It is about to appear eight times in a row.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the ending alone — \textquotedblleft{}zehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item the rule — \textquotedblleft{}a digit, then zehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item run it once — \textquotedblleft{}drei\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}zehn\textquotedblright{}, then the two joined
  \item what English hides — \textquotedblleft{}-teen is ten\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ziffer plus zehn.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the rule? (\textbf{A digit, then} \emph{zehn}.) Does anything go between them? (\textbf{No}.) Run it on \emph{drei} and say what comes out. How does every one of them end? (\emph{\textbf{-tsayn}}.) And what is English \emph{-teen}? (\emph{\textbf{Ten}}.) Next: the rule's first run.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dreizehn]{dreizehn — \textquotedblleft{}thirteen\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-dreizehn}



\begin{quote}
You have the rule and you have the digit. Say the number before you read it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dreizehn}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{dreizehn} — \textquotedblleft{}thirteen.\textquotedblright{} \emph{drei} + \emph{zehn}.
\end{quote}

Nothing added, nothing changed. If you predicted it, that is the point of the chapter working.

English wore its digit down — \emph{three} became \emph{thir-} — and German did not touch its own.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ei} — \emph{ei} is the vowel of English \textbf{eye}, unchanged from \emph{drei}.
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — and the second half is \emph{-TSAYN}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{DREI-tsayn}, with the weight on the digit, not the ending. That stress pattern holds for every number in this chapter.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the parts — \textquotedblleft{}drei, zehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item joined — \textquotedblleft{}dreizehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English one and its worn-down digit — \textquotedblleft{}thirteen, from three\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}drei, zehn, dreizehn.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}thirteen.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Dreizehn}}.) What are its halves? (\emph{\textbf{Drei}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{zehn}}.) Did either change? (\textbf{No}.) Which syllable is stressed? (\textbf{The first} — the digit.) Next: fourteen, the same way.
\end{tcolorbox}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-vierzehn}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{vierzehn} — \textquotedblleft{}fourteen.\textquotedblright{} \emph{vier} + \emph{zehn}.
\end{quote}

  \item \texttt{z-ts} — and \emph{-TSAYN} again.
\end{itemize}

\emph{FEER-tsayn}. Third time for that \emph{v}: a number, a father, and now a teen.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the parts — \textquotedblleft{}vier, zehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item joined — \textquotedblleft{}vierzehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two so far — \textquotedblleft{}dreizehn, vierzehn\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}fourteen.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Vierzehn}}.) How is the \emph{V} said? (\textbf{As an} \emph{f}.) What are its halves? (\emph{\textbf{Vier}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{zehn}}.) Next: fifteen.

\section[fünfzehn]{fünfzehn — \textquotedblleft{}fifteen\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-fuenfzehn}



\begin{quote}
Third run of the rule, and the first place English is the messier of the two languages.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fünfzehn}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{fünfzehn} — \textquotedblleft{}fifteen.\textquotedblright{} \emph{fünf} + \emph{zehn}.
\end{quote}

The digit is whole. English is not: \textbf{five} became \emph{fif-}, so \emph{fifteen} no longer shows its own number. German keeps \emph{fünf} visible and audible.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{umlaut-ue} — the \emph{ü} from \emph{fünf}, unchanged: say \emph{ee}, then round the lips.
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — and \emph{-TSAYN}.
\end{itemize}

Two syllables, the weight on \emph{fünf} and the ending unstressed.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the parts — \textquotedblleft{}fünf, zehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item joined — \textquotedblleft{}fünfzehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item three in a row — \textquotedblleft{}dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item what English lost — \textquotedblleft{}five became fif-\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}fifteen.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Fünfzehn}}.) Is the digit whole? (\textbf{Yes}.) Is English's? (\textbf{No} — \emph{five} \textbf{became} \emph{fif-}.) Say the three you have. (\textbf{Dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn}.) Next: where German clips too.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[die Klippung]{The two clipped digits}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-klippung}



\begin{quote}
The rule holds for every number in this chapter. Two of them shorten the digit first, and it is worth knowing which before you meet them.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two digits get shortened}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the digit} & \textbf{before \emph{zehn} it becomes} & \textbf{why} \\
\midrule
\emph{sechs} & \emph{sech-} & the \emph{s} would collide with the \emph{ts} of \emph{zehn} \\
\emph{sieben} & \emph{sieb-} & the \emph{-en} is an unstressed syllable too many \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both are the mouth economising, not the grammar changing. It is still a digit with \emph{zehn} on the end; the digit has been worn smooth at the join and nothing more.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
English did the same thing and did more of it. \emph{Three} became \emph{thir-} and \emph{five} became \emph{fif-}, and nobody thinks of \emph{thirteen} as irregular — it is a worn compound, exactly like these two.

So the honest scoreboard is: \textbf{English clips two digits, German clips two digits, and they are not the same two.} German keeps \emph{fünf} whole where English does not; English keeps \emph{six} and \emph{seven} whole where German does not. Neither language is tidier. Both are old, and old words get worn.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the full digits — \textquotedblleft{}sechs, sieben\textquotedblright{}
  \item their clipped forms — \textquotedblleft{}sech-, sieb-\textquotedblright{}
  \item what English clipped instead — \textquotedblleft{}three to thir-, five to fif-\textquotedblright{}
  \item what has not changed — \textquotedblleft{}still a digit, then zehn\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}sechs to sech-, sieben to sieb-.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two German digits shorten? (\emph{\textbf{Sechs}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{sieben}}.) What do they become? (\emph{\textbf{Sech-}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{sieb-}}.) Is the rule broken? (\textbf{No} — the digit is worn, the rule holds.) Which two did English clip? (\emph{\textbf{Three}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{five}}.) Next: the first of the two.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sechzehn]{sechzehn — \textquotedblleft{}sixteen\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-sechzehn}



\begin{quote}
First of the two clipped ones. You already know what it drops.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sechzehn}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sechzehn} — \textquotedblleft{}sixteen.\textquotedblright{} \emph{sech-} + \emph{zehn}, with the \emph{s} of \emph{sechs} gone.
\end{quote}

Try it with the \emph{s} left in and you will hear the problem: \emph{sechs-zehn} puts an \emph{s} immediately before a \emph{ts}, and the two will not sit next to each other.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ch-ach} — the \emph{ch} is the raspy one from \emph{acht} and \emph{Nacht}, made at the back.
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — and then straight into \emph{-TSAYN}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{ZECH-tsayn}, where the first sound is the buzzed German \emph{s}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole digit — \textquotedblleft{}sechs\textquotedblright{}
  \item the clipped one — \textquotedblleft{}sech-\textquotedblright{}
  \item the number — \textquotedblleft{}sechzehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item four in a row — \textquotedblleft{}dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn, sechzehn\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}sechs, sechzehn.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}sixteen.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Sechzehn}}.) What did the digit lose? (\textbf{Its} \emph{s}.) Why? (\textbf{It would collide with the} \emph{ts}.) Is the rule still digit + \emph{zehn}? (\textbf{Yes}.) Next: the other clipped one.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[siebzehn]{siebzehn — \textquotedblleft{}seventeen\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-siebzehn}



\begin{quote}
Second and last of the clipped ones. After this the rule runs clean to twenty.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: siebzehn}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{siebzehn} — \textquotedblleft{}seventeen.\textquotedblright{} \emph{sieb-} + \emph{zehn}, with the \emph{-en} of \emph{sieben} gone.
\end{quote}

\emph{Sieben-zehn} would be four syllables for one number, three of them unstressed. German trimmed the middle and kept the meaning.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ie-long-ee} — \emph{ie} is a long \textbf{ee}, as in \emph{sieben}.
  \item \texttt{consonant-b-final} — the \emph{b} stays a \emph{b} here, because it is not really at the end of a word: \emph{zehn} is welded on behind it.
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — and \emph{-TSAYN}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{ZEEB-tsayn}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole digit — \textquotedblleft{}sieben\textquotedblright{}
  \item the clipped one — \textquotedblleft{}sieb-\textquotedblright{}
  \item the number — \textquotedblleft{}siebzehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two clipped ones together — \textquotedblleft{}sechzehn, siebzehn\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}sieben, siebzehn.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}seventeen.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Siebzehn}}.) What did the digit lose? (\textbf{Its} \emph{-en}.) Name both clipped numbers. (\emph{\textbf{Sechzehn\emph{, }siebzehn}}.) How many are left to clip? (\textbf{None}.) Next: eighteen, whole again.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[achtzehn]{achtzehn — \textquotedblleft{}eighteen\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-achtzehn}



\begin{quote}
The clipping is over. From here the digits go in whole.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: achtzehn}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{achtzehn} — \textquotedblleft{}eighteen.\textquotedblright{} \emph{acht} + \emph{zehn}, both whole.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ch-ach} — the raspy \emph{ch} of \emph{acht}, unchanged.
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — and \emph{-TSAYN}.
\end{itemize}

That \emph{-cht} is the one you were given twice: \emph{acht} against English \textbf{eight}, \emph{Nacht} against \textbf{night}. Where German rasps, English writes \emph{-ght} and says nothing at all.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the parts — \textquotedblleft{}acht, zehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item joined — \textquotedblleft{}achtzehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair that shares the rasp — \textquotedblleft{}acht, Nacht\textquotedblright{}
  \item their silent English twins — \textquotedblleft{}eight, night\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}acht, achtzehn.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}eighteen.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Achtzehn}}.) Was the digit clipped? (\textbf{No} — whole.) What does English write where German rasps? (\emph{\textbf{-ght}}.) Next: nineteen.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[neunzehn]{neunzehn — \textquotedblleft{}nineteen\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-neunzehn}



\begin{quote}
Eighth and last run of the rule. You should be able to say it before reading on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: neunzehn}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{neunzehn} — \textquotedblleft{}nineteen.\textquotedblright{} \emph{neun} + \emph{zehn}, both whole.
\end{quote}

Seven numbers built from one rule and not one of them broke it. Two shortened a digit at the join and kept the rule intact.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-eu} — \emph{eu} is the \emph{oy} of English \emph{boy}, unchanged from \emph{neun}.
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — and \emph{-TSAYN} for the last time.
\end{itemize}

\emph{NOYN-tsayn}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the parts — \textquotedblleft{}neun, zehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item joined — \textquotedblleft{}neunzehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item the last four — \textquotedblleft{}sechzehn, siebzehn, achtzehn, neunzehn\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}achtzehn, neunzehn.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}nineteen.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Neunzehn}}.) Its halves? (\emph{\textbf{Neun}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{zehn}}.) How many numbers has the rule built? (\textbf{Seven}.) How many times did it break? (\textbf{None}.) Next: twenty, which stops using \emph{zehn}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zwanzig]{zwanzig — \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-zwanzig}



\begin{quote}
Eight numbers ended in \emph{zehn}. This one does not, and the ending it takes instead is worth a lesson of its own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: zwanzig}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{zwanzig} — \textquotedblleft{}twenty.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

It opens like \emph{zwei} and \emph{zwölf} — \emph{tsv-} — and then closes on \textbf{-zig} where every number before it closed on \emph{-zehn}.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — twice: \emph{tsv-} at the front, \emph{-ts-} in the middle.
  \item \texttt{w-as-v} — the \emph{w} is a \textbf{v}, as always.
  \item \texttt{ich-laut} — and the final \emph{-ig} is said as the soft \emph{ich}-sound from the very first chapters: \emph{-ikh}, not \emph{-ig}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{TSVAHN-tsikh}. That final \emph{-ig} rule holds for every German word ending the same way, so it is worth more than this one number.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the ending alone — \textquotedblleft{}-ikh\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}zwanzig\textquotedblright{} — TSVAHN-tsikh
  \item the last two — \textquotedblleft{}neunzehn, zwanzig\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three that open the same way — \textquotedblleft{}zwei, zwölf, zwanzig\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}neunzehn, zwanzig.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}twenty.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Zwanzig}}.) How does the ending sound? (\emph{\textbf{-ikh}} — the soft \emph{ich}-sound.) Does it end in \emph{zehn}? (\textbf{No} — \emph{-zig}.) Which number is at the front? (\emph{\textbf{Zwei}}.) Next: what \emph{-zig} actually is.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-zig und -ty]{-zig and -ty}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-zwanzig-zwei-zehn}



\begin{quote}
The ending changed at twenty. It did not change subject.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Older Germanic \emph{twaintig}, which is \emph{twain} — \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} — plus \emph{tig}, and \emph{\textbf{tig\emph{ is ten\textbf{.}}}}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{is} & \textbf{and means} \\
\midrule
\emph{zwanzig} & \emph{zwei} + \emph{-zig} & two tens \\
twenty & twain + \emph{-ty} & two tens \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{-zig} and \emph{-ty} are the \textbf{same ending}, both of them \emph{ten} worn down by being said a great many times. German's \emph{zehn} stayed whole because it kept being used on its own; the version welded onto twenty wore out instead.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Stand back and the whole span from eleven to twenty is three ideas, and you have all three.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Eleven and twelve} count what is \emph{left over} after ten fingers.
  \item \textbf{Thirteen to nineteen} are a digit with \emph{ten} on the end.
  \item \textbf{Twenty} is \emph{two tens}, with the same \emph{ten} worn to \emph{-zig}.
\end{itemize}

Every one of those is a compound. Not one number in this chapter is a word you had to be given — they are all built, and the parts were yours before the chapter started.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what twenty is — \textquotedblleft{}two tens\textquotedblright{}
  \item the German pair — \textquotedblleft{}zwei, zwanzig\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English pair — \textquotedblleft{}twain, twenty\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two endings that are one word — \textquotedblleft{}-zig, -ty, both ten\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}zwanzig — two tens.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{zwanzig} mean underneath? (\textbf{Two tens}.) What is \emph{-zig}? (\emph{\textbf{Ten}}, \textbf{worn down}.) And English \emph{-ty}? (\textbf{The same word}.) So how many of this chapter's numbers are compounds? (\textbf{All of them}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — thirteen to twenty}

\label{lesson:GE-C12-zahlen-13-20}



\begin{quote}
No new words. One rule, run eight times, and two small wearings-down along the way.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the rule and its two exceptions that are not exceptions}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{digit} & \textbf{joined} \\
\midrule
13 & \emph{drei} & \emph{dreizehn} \\
14 & \emph{vier} & \emph{vierzehn} \\
15 & \emph{fünf} & \emph{fünfzehn} \\
16 & \emph{sech-} & \emph{sechzehn} \\
17 & \emph{sieb-} & \emph{siebzehn} \\
18 & \emph{acht} & \emph{achtzehn} \\
19 & \emph{neun} & \emph{neunzehn} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Six digits go in whole and two are trimmed at the join. The rule never changes.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Eleven to twenty is three ideas and you now hold all three: two \textbf{leftovers}, seven \textbf{digit-plus-ten} compounds, and one \textbf{two-tens}.

Here is the contrast worth carrying. The Romance sisters all \textbf{break} partway through the teens and switch to a different construction — Portuguese at sixteen, French and Italian at seventeen. German does not break at all. Two leftovers, then one clean rule to twenty, and English marches beside it the whole distance because it is doing the same thing with the same worn-down words.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item count from thirteen — \textquotedblleft{}dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn, sechzehn, siebzehn, achtzehn, neunzehn, zwanzig\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two trimmed digits — \textquotedblleft{}sech-, sieb-\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one that stops using zehn — \textquotedblleft{}zwanzig\textquotedblright{}
  \item count the whole span — \textquotedblleft{}elf, zwölf, dreizehn … zwanzig\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn, sechzehn.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the rule from thirteen up? (\textbf{A digit, then} \emph{zehn}.) Which two digits are trimmed? (\emph{\textbf{Sechs}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{sieben}}.) Does the rule ever break? (\textbf{No}.) What is \emph{zwanzig} underneath? (\textbf{Two tens}.) And where do the Romance languages break? (\textbf{Partway through the teens} — sixteen or seventeen.)
\end{tcolorbox}
